Sparta. An austere warrior society located in the Peloponnese that dominated the classical Greek world through military might and iron discipline rather than intellectual or artistic achievement. Built on a rigid caste system with helots—enslaved subjects—toiling below a warrior aristocracy, Sparta became Athens's great rival and the supreme land power of ancient Greece.

Sparta was governed by a dual monarchy with two hereditary kings ruling jointly, along with a council of elders. This system was unique among Greek city-states. Young Spartan boys were subjected to the Agoge, a brutal state-sponsored military training regime beginning at age seven. This system stripped them of individuality and forged them into efficient soldiers.

The entire society was grounded in a warrior ethos. Spartans valued death in battle above surrender, summarized by a famous phrase: come back with your shield or on it—meaning never retreat, only advance or die. Sparta defeated the Persian Empire at Thermopylae in 480 BCE, where Leonidas and three hundred hoplites held the pass against the vast army of Xerxes. Against overwhelming odds, they fought to the death, becoming legendary for their courage.

Sparta emerged victorious in the Peloponnesian War against Athens, lasting from 431 to 404 BCE, and became the dominant power in Greece for several decades. The city employed a powerful navy of triremes—three-banked warships—and forged alliances through the Peloponnesian League.

Sparta deliberately remained isolated from arts and philosophy, viewing such pursuits as weaknesses that would undermine martial virtue. The city produced no dramatists or major philosophers of note. Athens was Sparta's supreme rival and opponent in the Peloponnesian War. Leonidas was the Spartan king who led the stand at Thermopylae. The hoplite was the Greek warrior type, perfected and epitomized by Spartan soldiers. The Peloponnese was the geographical region where Sparta was located and dominant.
